title: She was called unclean for something God created—but did God ever call her sinful?
paragraphs: SHE WAS CALLED UNCLEAN FOR SOMETHING GOD CREATED—BUT DID GOD EVER CALL HER SINFUL? What Leviticus 15:19–23 actually teaches about menstruation, the difference between impurity and sin, and the breathtaking moment Jesus confronted centuries of human shame. Imagine being a woman who wakes up one morning bleeding. You haven't disobeyed God. You haven't committed adultery. You haven't stolen anything, entertained wicked desires, or deliberately rebelled against heaven.

Your body is simply doing what it was biologically designed to do. Yet under the Mosaic Law, the bed you sleep on becomes ritually unclean. The chair you sit on becomes ritually unclean. Anyone who touches you becomes ritually unclean until evening. Now imagine someone looking into your eyes and telling you that your very existence during those seven days makes you spiritually disgusting. Would you believe them? Would you begin apologizing for the body God gave you?

Would you start wondering whether God was ashamed of creating you? Because somewhere between what Scripture actually says and what human beings have made it mean, countless women have carried a burden God never declared to be a moral offense. And the distinction could change the way you understand not only Leviticus but the entire Gospel of Jesus Christ.

Leviticus 15:19–23 begins with these words in the original Hebrew: וְאִשָּׁה כִּי־תִהְיֶה זָבָה דָּם יִהְיֶה זֹבָהּ בִּבְשָׂרָהּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים תִּהְיֶה בְנִדָּתָהּ Ve'ishah ki tihyeh zavah, dam yihyeh zovah bivsarah, shiv'at yamim tihyeh beniddatah. A close translation reads: “When a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her menstrual impurity for seven days.”

The passage continues by explaining that anyone who touches her becomes unclean until evening, and that objects upon which she lies or sits become ritually unclean. Those who touch her bedding or the objects on which she sits must wash their clothes, bathe in water, and remain unclean until evening. There is no denying what the passage says. But there is also no justification for making it say something it doesn't.

One of the most important Hebrew words in this passage is נִדָּה (niddah), a term associated in this context with menstruation and the resulting state of ritual impurity. Another is טָמֵא (tameʾ), meaning unclean or impure. In the context of Leviticus 15, this uncleanness is a ritual condition. It is not, by itself, a declaration of moral guilt. That distinction matters enormously. Because being ritually unclean was not automatically the same thing as being sinful.

A woman could be ritually unclean without having committed a single sin by menstruating. Read that again. God was not commanding women to repent for having menstrual cycles. He was not accusing them of rebellion because their bodies were bleeding. He was not declaring that femininity was a spiritual defect. In fact, Leviticus 15 itself dismantles the idea that ritual impurity was exclusively a female problem. The chapter begins by addressing male bodily discharges.

Leviticus 15:16–18 explains that an emission of semen could also produce temporary ritual uncleanness, including after marital intercourse. Childbirth resulted in ritual impurity under Leviticus 12. Contact with a dead body produced ritual impurity under Numbers 19:11. Think about that. A mother could become ritually unclean after bringing a new life into the world. A grieving person could become ritually unclean after touching the body of someone they loved.

A husband and wife could become ritually unclean after an act of marital intimacy that was not inherently sinful. These were conditions of embodied human existence, not necessarily acts of moral rebellion. The Old Testament purity system distinguished between the holy and the common, and between the clean and the unclean, as Leviticus 10:10 explicitly teaches. These categories governed Israel's relationship with sacred spaces and worship under the Mosaic covenant.

Leviticus 15:31 explains the seriousness of these regulations by connecting Israel's impurity with the danger of defiling God's tabernacle. God's holiness was not casual. His presence was not something Israel could approach carelessly. Disobedience to the purity regulations could carry moral consequences, but that does not mean the natural bodily condition itself was a sin.

And although scholars have discussed the symbolic relationship between blood, life, bodily discharges, and mortality, Scripture does not provide an exhaustive explanation for every detail of these regulations. We must be careful not to present speculation as divine revelation. What we can say with confidence is that the Bible never identifies ordinary menstruation itself as an act of moral wrongdoing. Yet human beings have an extraordinary ability to turn religious distinctions into personal condemnation.

We take a condition and turn it into an identity. We take someone's suffering and turn it into an accusation. We take something a person cannot control and convince them that they should be ashamed of it. And sometimes we do it while holding a Bible. Perhaps you know exactly what that feels like. Maybe you grew up believing that your period made you spiritually dirty. Perhaps someone told you that God was less willing to hear your prayers during those days.

Maybe you were embarrassed to speak about your own body, even when you were in pain. Or perhaps your shame has nothing to do with menstruation. Perhaps it is your infertility. Your chronic illness. Your disability. Your scars. The condition you desperately wish would disappear. The weakness you have prayed about so many times that you have almost become afraid to pray again. Somewhere along the way, you began confusing what was happening to you with who you were before God.

And that is where the story becomes astonishing. Centuries after the regulations of Leviticus were given, a woman appeared in the Gospel of Mark. We are never told her name. But we are told something about her suffering that is almost unbearable to imagine. She had been bleeding for twelve years. Not seven days. Not several weeks. Twelve years. Mark 5:25 describes her condition in Greek: Καὶ γυνὴ οὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος δώδεκα ἔτη Kai gynē ousa en rhysei haimatos dōdeka etē.

“And a woman who had been suffering from a flow of blood for twelve years.” Her condition was not ordinary menstruation. It was a prolonged discharge of blood, corresponding more closely to the circumstances described in Leviticus 15:25–30. Under those regulations, her impurity would continue throughout the discharge. Mark tells us that she had suffered under many physicians, spent everything she had, and instead of getting better, had grown worse. Her money was gone. Her healing had not come.

Her condition remained. Scripture does not tell us every detail of her social life, so we cannot claim with certainty that she was completely abandoned by her family or permanently excluded from every community gathering. But the ritual implications of her condition, combined with years of physical suffering and financial exhaustion, help us understand the enormous weight she may have carried. Twelve years is a long time to suffer.

Long enough to watch other people move forward while you remain trapped in the same struggle. Long enough to become tired of explaining yourself. Long enough to wonder whether your prayers are reaching heaven. Long enough for suffering to begin feeling like your name. Then she heard about Jesus. She approached Him from behind, moving through the crowd. She did not deliver an impressive speech. She did not present a religious résumé. She did not arrive with proof that she deserved a miracle.

She simply believed that touching His clothing could make her well. Mark 5:28 records her words: “If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole.” — KJV And she touched Him. Immediately, the flow of blood stopped. But Jesus did something that makes this encounter even more beautiful. He stopped. He asked who had touched His clothes. The disciples were confused because people were pressing against Him from every direction. But Jesus knew that power had gone out from Him.

The woman came forward, trembling with fear, fell before Him, and told Him the whole truth. Imagine that moment. The condition she had endured for twelve years was now being brought into the open. Would she be rebuked? Would she be humiliated? Would she be treated as a contamination to be avoided? Listen carefully to what Jesus actually said. Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην. Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se; hypage eis eirēnēn. “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”

— Mark 5:34, close translation. Daughter. Not disgusting. Not defective. Not unwanted. Not a spiritual embarrassment. Daughter. The Greek word θυγάτηρ (thygatēr) means daughter. It is a deeply personal form of address in this encounter. The verb σέσωκέν (sesōken), from sōzō, can mean to save, rescue, heal, or make well. Here, the immediate context clearly includes her physical healing. Jesus did not merely allow her to disappear anonymously into the crowd after receiving a miracle. He acknowledged her.

He spoke peace over her. He publicly addressed her with tenderness. The woman who approached trembling left with the assurance of Christ's words. And here is the extraordinary contrast. In Leviticus, contact with certain bodily discharges communicated ritual impurity. In Mark, the encounter with Jesus results in healing flowing toward the suffering woman. The Gospel does not explicitly discuss Jesus' ritual status following this encounter. What it emphasizes is His authority, compassion, and power to heal.

Her suffering did not overpower Him. His healing overcame her suffering. That is not a contradiction between the God of Leviticus and the Jesus of the Gospels. It is a beautiful revelation of the redemptive story unfolding throughout Scripture. Jesus did not come because the Old Testament was a mistake. He declared in Matthew 5:17 that He came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them. The purity regulations belonged to Israel's covenantal system of holiness and worship.

Through Christ, the New Testament reveals the fulfillment of that system and a greater cleansing accomplished through His sacrifice. Hebrews 9:13–14 contrasts ceremonial purification with the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience so that we may serve the living God. Something deeper than ceremonial cleanliness was always needed to address humanity's greatest problem. Sin. And menstruation was never that problem.

Jesus teaches in Mark 7:20–23 that moral defilement comes from within the human heart: evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, deceit, pride, and other evils. Notice what He does not identify as a moral offense. The natural menstrual cycle of a woman. The tragedy is that some people have spent more energy condemning women's biological functions than confronting the pride, cruelty, hypocrisy, and judgment living inside their own hearts.

A woman may be menstruating while sincerely worshiping God. Meanwhile, someone standing beside her may be physically healthy but harboring bitterness, arrogance, or hatred. Which condition actually requires repentance? Scripture gives us the answer. This does not mean that sin is imaginary or that repentance is unnecessary. Quite the opposite. The Gospel calls every one of us to repent of genuine sin, receive forgiveness through Jesus Christ, and live transformed lives through His grace.

But repentance must be directed toward what God actually identifies as sin—not toward innocent bodily functions that human beings have surrounded with shame. We must never confuse the conviction of the Holy Spirit with condemnation manufactured by human prejudice. There is a difference between a conscience awakened to wrongdoing and a wounded person being taught to despise their own existence. Perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something they should have been told years ago.

You do not need to repent for menstruating. You do not become less valuable to God because you are bleeding. Your menstrual cycle does not invalidate your prayers. It does not disqualify you from Christian worship. It does not make you less worthy of dignity, compassion, or love. Under the new covenant, believers approach God through Jesus Christ, not through the maintenance of the Mosaic system of ceremonial purity.

Hebrews 10:19–22 invites believers to draw near to God through the blood of Jesus, with sincere hearts and the assurance of faith. Your access to the Father rests upon Christ's finished work. Not upon the calendar of your menstrual cycle. And if you are experiencing prolonged or unusually heavy bleeding, please seek appropriate medical care. Faith in Christ and responsible medical treatment are not enemies.

The woman in Mark received a miraculous healing, but Scripture does not promise that every believer will experience immediate physical healing in this present life. Even when healing takes time, and even when suffering remains, Christ's love is not diminished. Romans 8:38–39 reminds us that nothing in all creation can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus. What a different world we could create if Christians understood these truths before speaking into someone else's suffering.

How many daughters would grow up without unnecessary shame? How many mothers would stop apologizing for their bodies? How many wounded believers would return to prayer instead of hiding from the God they mistakenly believed was disgusted by them? How many people would discover that biblical holiness does not require us to invent new reasons to condemn one another? Never forget the woman in Mark's Gospel. Twelve years of bleeding. Twelve years of suffering. One encounter with Jesus.

And one word that still speaks across the centuries. Daughter. Leviticus described her ritual condition. Jesus demonstrated that her suffering did not place her beyond His compassion. The cross would reveal something even greater: that the genuine guilt of sinners could be forgiven, that the conscience could be cleansed, and that those who trust in Christ could draw near to God through His redeeming blood. There is no need to manufacture sins where God has not declared them.

There are enough real sins for which we desperately need His mercy. Bring those sins to Jesus. Bring your suffering to Jesus. Bring your questions, your wounds, your fears, and the shame you never knew how to explain. He is not confused about the difference between your need for forgiveness and your need for compassion. And neither should His people be. Never mistake the blood your body naturally sheds for the sin that required Christ to shed His.
